items.title: Integration against a Dirac measure evaluates at its point
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a set $X$, let $x_0\in X$, and let
$\delta_{x_0}$ be the Dirac probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For every
nonnegative $\mathcal A$-measurable $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_X f\,d\delta_{x_0}=f(x_0).$$

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis, Example 2.55
Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, Example 1.4.29

items.strategy: Reduce to nonnegative simple functions, evaluate each using the Dirac set function, then pass to the pointwise increasing limit by monotone convergence.

items.title: A statistic induces a deterministic probability kernel
items.statement:
Let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable
statistic, where $\mathcal G$ is a sigma-algebra on the action set
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). Then
$$K_T(x,B):=\delta_{T(x)}(B)=\mathbf 1_B(T(x)),\qquad x\in\mathcal X,\ B\in\mathcal G,$$
is a probability kernel and therefore a deterministic randomized procedure.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §5.1, PDF pp. 100–102
Peter Hoff, Statistical Decision Problems, §§2–4.2, PDF pp. 2–8

items.strategy: Check the probability-measure section at every data point and the measurability of each event evaluation.

items.title: Bias and mean squared error
items.statement:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment: a measurable data space, a parameter-label set,
and a family of probability measures on the data space. Let
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be its real-valued target function (estimand). An estimator
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is a measurable statistic
with the real Borel target ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). At a parameter
$\theta$ for which $T$ is integrable under $P_\theta$, its **bias** is
$$\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\psi(\theta).$$

Its **mean squared error** (MSE) is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
This is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by $T$ under squared-error
loss $L(\theta,a)=(a-\psi(\theta))^2$: its Dirac kernel is constructed in
[[lem-statistic-induces-deterministic-procedure]], and the risk supplier's
integral formula reduces to the displayed expectation when the action is
$T(x)$ by [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]
([[def-loss-function-and-risk]]). For each fixed $\theta$, this loss is Borel
in the real action $a$; no measurable structure on $\Theta$ or measurability
of $\psi$ is required. The expectation convention is
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. If $T$ is
square-integrable under $P_\theta$, then its variance is defined by
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and this MSE is finite. Bias is not
defined at parameters where $T$ is not integrable.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 5, PDF pp. 29–31
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 2–8
Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §5.1, PDF pp. 100–102

items.title: Bias–variance decomposition
items.statement:
In a statistical experiment, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and let $T$ be a
real estimator with $\mathbb E_\theta[T^2]<\infty$. For every $\theta$,
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2.$$

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 5, PDF pp. 29–31
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 2–8

items.strategy: Write estimation error as centered noise plus bias, expand its square, and use the centered term’s zero expectation.

items.title: Unbiased estimators and UMVU estimators
items.statement:
Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Definition 5.2, PDF pp. 29–30
Jun Shao, STAT 709 Lecture 15: UMVUE, PDF pp. 1–3
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 2–8

items.title: Rao–Blackwell theorem for scalar finite-variance estimators
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the library conditional-expectation
convention. Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ have
standard-Borel data space, let $\mathsf S$ be standard Borel, and let
$S:\mathcal X\to\mathsf S$ be a sufficient statistic. Here sufficiency uses
a **supplied common kernel** $K(s,\cdot)$ that is a regular conditional law of
the data given $S=s$ under every $P_\theta$ and does not depend on $\theta$
([[def-sufficient-statistic]]). For Borel $B\subseteq\mathsf S$, write $P_\theta^S(B):=P_\theta(S^{-1}(B))$ for the pushforward law of $S$. Let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and let $U$ be
a measurable real estimator with $\mathbb E_\theta[U]=\psi(\theta)$ and
$\mathbb E_\theta[U^2]<\infty$ for every $\theta$.

There is a single Borel function $g:\mathsf S\to\mathbb R$, independent of
$\theta$, such that $g(S)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E_\theta[U\mid\sigma(S)]$ for every $\theta$. It is unbiased,
finite-variance, and
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
For each $\theta$, equality holds exactly when $U$ is
$\sigma(S)$-measurable $P_\theta$-almost surely.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Theorem 6.1 and proof, PDF pp. 33–35
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 9–11
Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, Theorem 5.1 and proof, PDF pp. 102–103

items.strategy: Use the common sufficient-statistic kernel to construct one parameter-free conditional mean, then apply conditional expectation and L2 orthogonality.

items.title: Lehmann–Scheffé theorem
items.statement:
Assume AC as in the library conditional-expectation convention. Let
$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be
a statistical experiment with standard-Borel data space. Let
$S:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathsf S,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with
standard-Borel target, sufficient under the common conditional-law interface
of [[def-sufficient-statistic]] and complete under [[def-complete-statistic]].
Let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued estimand and let
$g:\mathsf S\to\mathbb R$ be Borel, with $g(S)$ unbiased for $\psi$ and of
finite variance under every $P_\theta$. Then $g(S)$ is the unique UMVU
estimator of $\psi$: for every finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta),$$
and any other UMVU estimator equals $g(S)$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for each
$\theta$.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Theorem 6.5 and proof, PDF pp. 37–38
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 15–16
Jun Shao, STAT 709 Lecture 15: UMVUE, PDF pp. 1–4

items.strategy: Rao–Blackwellize each unbiased competitor, use completeness on the difference of functions of the sufficient statistic, and use the equality case for uniqueness.

items.title: The binomial sample proportion
items.statement:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent Bernoulli$(p)$ observations, where
$n\geq1$ and $p\in[0,1]$. For $\overline X=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$,
$$\mathbb E_p[\overline X]=p,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_p(\overline X)=\operatorname{MSE}_p(\overline X)=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.$$
The equalities include the degenerate endpoints $p=0$ and $p=1$.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 5, PDF pp. 29–31
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 2–8

items.strategy: Compute Bernoulli moments, use independence to remove cross covariances, and apply the bias–variance identity.

items.title: A biased estimator can have lower MSE
items.statement:
Observe one $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ and estimate $p$. The unbiased
estimator $T_1=X$ has $\operatorname{MSE}_p(T_1)=p(1-p)$. The constant
estimator $T_0=0$ is biased when $p>0$, but at $p=1/5$,
$$\operatorname{MSE}_{1/5}(T_0)=\frac1{25}<\frac4{25}=\operatorname{MSE}_{1/5}(T_1).$$
This is a pointwise comparison at $p=1/5$, not a uniform improvement: at $p=1$
the constant rule has MSE $1$ and $T_1$ has MSE $0$.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Chapter 5, PDF pp. 29–31
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 2–8

items.strategy: Compute both Bernoulli risks and compare them at p=1/5; check p=1 to show the comparison is not uniform.

items.title: Rao–Blackwellizing one Bernoulli observation by the sample sum
items.statement:
Work on the finite product sample space $\{0,1\}^n$ with its discrete
sigma-algebra. Let its coordinates $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid Bernoulli$(p)$ with
$p\in[0,1]$, $n\geq1$, and $S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. The unbiased estimator $U=X_1$
is Rao–Blackwellized by $S$ to
$$\mathbb E_p[X_1\mid S]=\frac Sn.$$
The statistic $S$ is sufficient: conditional on $S=s$, the data vector is
uniform over the vectors with $s$ ones when $0<p<1$. At $p=0$ and $p=1$, only
the fibers $s=0$ and $s=n$ are supported, respectively, and their conditional
laws are point masses at the all-zero and all-one vectors. These conditional
laws do not depend on $p$.

references.title: George Deligiannidis, SB2.1 Foundations of Statistical Inference, Theorem 6.1 and Bernoulli example, PDF pp. 33–35
Karl B. Gregory, STAT 713 Lecture 6: Best Unbiased Estimators, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, PDF pp. 9–11

items.strategy: Verify the common conditional law on each sample-sum fiber and use permutation symmetry to compute the conditional mean.
